Name: Steve Heckman
Question: Can 110 volts kill me? If so, does it take time? I touched a transformer and I’m worried.
Answer: Under the right conditions, 110 VAC can kill you. But the death is fairly immediate. Getting zapped and then dying later? Not so much. The only time I’ve seen people die later were due to complications (burns) and that was with significantly higher voltages. In all cases I’m aware of involve construction workers or linemen making contact with the 5KV (or higher) distribution lines. Given this is a five year old question, we should know by now that it carried no long-term ill effects. If at work, use lock-out tag-out procedures well as PPE. And have a coworker present, preferable without a camera. On the other hand, you might get a new hairdo!

Name: Steve Heckman
Question: If you could travel back in time and witness any event in history, what would it be and what would you hope to learn from the experience?
Answer: First, I would not want to witness any disaster that occured, as knowing the outcome and yet not being able to do anything to stop it would not do well for my mental health. So, probably I’d want to go back and watch the launch of Apollo 11, and then retire to a motel room for a few days and watch the rest of the mission on TV. I know there was no time specified, but I’d like to watch the entire mission on TV before I went back to the future. That would allow some family visits and sightseeing along the way, maybe visits some restaurants in my hometown that no longer exist. I’d need a cool cover story though, to explain why I’m showing up. I dont think “I’m a time traveler” is going to cut it. My grandparents witnessed a later Apollo launch, on a trip they took when my grandfather retired.

Name: Steve Heckman
Question: Which engineering discipline combines most disciplines?
Answer: While there is some overlap between all engineer disciplines, there are two that stand out in my mind… First is biomedical engineering. I am fond of saying that engineering is applied physics, but biomedical engineering adds biology to the mix. The major complaint with biomedical engineering is it lacks “depth” as you are covering so much material, you never do a deep dive into any single area. Second is mechatronics. It is also a relatively “new” field that combines mechanical, electrical, and computer control systems into one discipline. Though mechatronics has some of the same risks as biomedical (being broad) its main focus is on automation, where the various skills are needed at a systems-level. Everything from industrial robotics and vision systems, to autonomous cars and drones all fall under this discipline.

Name: Steve Heckman
Question: What are the benefits of having both a PhD in engineering and an MBA?
Answer: This is one of these “it really depends” answers! First, the MBA will set you up for a management track. Many engineers go on to earn one. That said, I seem many people recommend that you earn a MBA later, after working at least 10 years as an engineer. The reason for that is 1) 24-year-olds are NOT ready for leadership positions, even if daddy own the company and 2) by the time you are ready to lead, you have flushed a lot of what you have learned. Second, the PhD is a different animal. In some case it can hurt finding a rank-and-file engineering positions, as evidence shows that a Master’s in Engineering is the sweet spot for most engineer's careers. On the other hand, while earning a MBA by going to night school is fairly common and easy, earning a PhD takes a lot of commitment, and is best done when you are young and are willing to eat Raman noodles for several years. And while we are taking about the benefits, the process is also important. Nevertheless, a PhD in certain areas is of great benefit, as lots of large companies perform R&D. Now, we are speaking of engineering, not computer science (where AI research now is hot) but of course in the modern world there is lots of overlap in the various fields. And while there is a demand for PhDs, the job market is significantly smaller. Now, what about both? In some technology drive companies that could be a ticket to eventually earning a senior management role. And it also gives some credibility to startups seeking investment if one of the founders covers these bases (as one person, or divide up among the team) But remember that credential collection does not guarantee any future success. You could be well educated but have no common sense, especially outside the relatively safe academic world. I’m not suggesting you go either way. I dropped out of grad school, but otherwise did just fine. Oh, look, a comic about PhD’s!
